summary: This note covers the early career of Stevie Wonder, beginning with his work under producer and songwriter Clarence Paul over roughly a year. Two albums were recorded in that period: Tribute to Uncle Ray, mostly Ray Charles covers, and The Jazz Soul of Little Stevie, an instrumental album. Wonder's Motown debut single, 'I Call It Pretty Music, But the Old People Call It the Blues', came out in summer 1962 and barely charted, and the follow-up singles and albums also had little success.
one_line: Covers the early career of Stevie Wonder, from his 1961-62 recordings with Clarence Paul to his commercially unsuccessful 1962 debut single and albums.
key_facts: Stevie Wonder was put in the care of producer and songwriter Clarence Paul.
Wonder and Paul worked together for a year on two albums.
Tribute to Uncle Ray was recorded first, when Wonder was still 11 years old.
Tribute to Uncle Ray consisted mainly of covers of Ray Charles's songs and included the Wonder and Paul composition 'Sunset'.
The Jazz Soul of Little Stevie was an instrumental album consisting mainly of Clarence Paul's compositions.
'Wondering' and 'Session Number 112' were co-written by Paul and Wonder for The Jazz Soul of Little Stevie.
'Mother Thank You' was recorded for release as a single but was pulled and replaced.
The replacement debut single was 'I Call It Pretty Music, But the Old People Call It the Blues', a Berry Gordy song.
The debut single was released in summer 1962 and spent one week of August at 101 on the Billboard 100.
'Little Water Boy' and 'Contract on Love' were follow-up singles that had no success.
The Jazz Soul of Little Stevie was released in September 1962.
Tribute to Uncle Ray was released in October 1962, after The Jazz Soul of Little Stevie, despite being recorded first.
Both albums met with little success.
